Monument-Valley.verdict: A short, beautiful puzzle game where you bend impossible architecture to guide a silent princess to each exit.
Monument-Valley.bestFor: Players who want a calm, polished puzzle game they can finish over a weekend.
pros: Clean, striking visuals that look like moving illustrations
Puzzles are gentle and rarely leave you stuck for long
No ads, and the $3.99 price covers the main game
Rated Everyone, so it suits the whole family
cons: The main story is short and can be finished in a couple of hours
Has in-app purchases for extra chapters
Experienced puzzle fans may find it easy
body: You guide Ida, a small princess, through a series of structures built from optical illusions. Rotating a tower, sliding a bridge or turning a crank can link paths that looked disconnected. Everything is done by touch, so it feels natural on a phone.
The game has no timer and no penalty for mistakes, so you can take your time. The soundtrack and soft colors give it a relaxed feel, and the story is told with very little text.
It costs $3.99 up front with no ads, though it does include in-app purchases. It suits anyone who likes puzzles with atmosphere more than difficulty.
Monument-Valley.author: editors

Monument-Valley-2.verdict: A follow-up that keeps the illusion puzzles and adds a mother-and-child story with a few new tricks.
Monument-Valley-2.bestFor: Fans of the first game, or anyone who wants a short, quiet puzzle game with no purchases.
pros: Same striking art style, with new puzzle ideas
You guide two characters, which adds variety to the puzzles
No ads and no in-app purchases after the $3.99 price
Relaxed pacing with no timers
cons: Short, so it is quickly finished
Puzzles are still fairly easy
Feels familiar if you just played the first game
body: You play a mother and her child, moving them through shifting buildings by rotating and sliding parts of the scenery. At times the two split up, and you have to think about where each of them can stand.
The puzzles stay gentle, and the focus is on atmosphere, music and a simple story about growing up. It is easy to pick up for a short session.
At $3.99 with no ads and no in-app purchases, you pay once and that is it. It works well for players who want something relaxing, whether or not they played the first one.
Monument-Valley-2.author: editors

Terraria.verdict: A 2D sandbox where you dig, build, craft gear and fight bosses, all for one $4.99 payment.
Terraria.bestFor: Players who want a big, open-ended game with plenty of things to do for a one-time price.
pros: Large amount of content: mining, building, crafting and boss fights
No ads and no in-app purchases
Lets you play your own way, from builder to fighter
Good value at $4.99
cons: Rated Teen because of fantasy combat
Little guidance at the start, so new players may feel lost
Touch controls take some getting used to
body: You start in a randomly generated world with a few basic tools. You dig for ore, build a house, craft better weapons and armor, and take on enemies and bosses as you go deeper. Villagers move in once you build them homes.
There is no fixed path. Some players spend hours on building projects, while others focus on exploring caves and fighting bosses. Mobile multiplayer lets you play with friends.
It is a good fit for players who enjoy crafting and exploring and don't mind working things out. Because it has no ads or purchases, the $4.99 is all you spend.
Terraria.author: editors

Muse-Dash.verdict: A rhythm game where you tap and dodge along with upbeat songs as cute characters run through colorful stages.
Muse-Dash.bestFor: Rhythm game fans who like fast, cheerful music and simple tap controls.
pros: Easy to learn: you tap to hit enemies and avoid obstacles in time with the music
Upbeat soundtrack with a wide mix of electronic and pop styles
No ads, and a low $2.99 price
Several difficulty levels
cons: Includes in-app purchases, such as extra music packs
Higher difficulties can be very demanding
Rated Teen
body: Notes come toward your character along two lanes, one on the ground and one in the air. You tap the right side of the screen for the ground and the left for the sky, and some notes need you to hold or avoid them.
Each song has several difficulty levels, so beginners can start easy and push on later. Your character and a small helper give you different bonuses, and the cartoon style keeps the mood light.
It costs $2.99 and has no ads, but extra content can be bought in the game. It suits people who enjoy rhythm games and want short, replayable sessions.
Muse-Dash.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.verdict: A tense horror game where you watch cameras and vents to survive five nights against a single animatronic.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.bestFor: Horror fans who like slow, nerve-testing survival games rather than fast action.
pros: Tense atmosphere built on sound and limited information
One stalker animatronic makes each night feel different
No ads and no in-app purchases
Cheap at $2.99
cons: Jump scares make it unsuitable for younger players, and it is rated Teen
Short once you learn how to beat each night
Managing several systems at once can be frustrating
body: You work as a night guard in a haunted attraction, switching between camera views to track Springtrap. You also have to keep the ventilation, audio and other systems running, because they break down as the night goes on.
The game gives you very little to fight with, so you survive by watching, listening and reacting quickly. Some bonus minigames add more story if you want to dig into it.
It costs $2.99, with no ads or in-app purchases. It is best for players who already like this style of horror and want to play it on a phone.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.verdict: A horror game set in a child's bedroom where you listen for breathing and close doors to stay safe.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.bestFor: Players who enjoy sound-based horror and don't mind jump scares.
pros: Tension comes from listening, which works well with headphones
Simple idea: check doors, closet and bed, then react
No ads and no in-app purchases
Low price of $2.99
cons: Rated Teen, with frequent jump scares
Timing mistakes can end a night suddenly
Not much variety once you understand the routine
body: Instead of an office with cameras, you are in a bedroom with a closet, two doors and a hallway. You must check each spot and shut the door when you hear breathing, while watching for threats at the bed.
There are no cameras to rely on, so sound is your main clue. A flashlight is your only tool, and using it at the wrong time can get you caught.
At $2.99 with no ads or purchases, it is an inexpensive choice for horror fans. Newcomers may want to start with the earlier games to know what to expect.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.author: editors

Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.verdict: A free puzzle game where you pour colored water between tubes until each tube holds one color.
Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.bestFor: Anyone who wants a relaxed free puzzle game for short breaks.
pros: Easy rules that anyone can learn in a minute
Free to download and rated Everyone
Short levels suit quick sessions
Can be played one-handed
cons: Has ads between levels
Includes in-app purchases
Later levels can feel repetitive
body: Each level gives you a set of tubes filled with mixed layers of colored water. You tap a tube, then tap another to pour, but you can only pour onto the same color or into an empty tube.

The early levels are simple, and difficulty grows with more colors and fewer empty tubes. If you get stuck, you can usually undo moves or add a tube, and some of these helps may need ads or purchases.
It is free, so expect ads. It suits players who want something calm and low-pressure to fill a few minutes.
Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.author: editors

Nut-Sort-Color-Match-Game.verdict: A free sorting puzzle where you move colored nuts onto bolts until each bolt has one color.
Nut-Sort-Color-Match-Game.bestFor: Casual players who enjoy sorting puzzles and want something simple and free.
pros: Simple, familiar sorting idea that is easy to pick up
Free and rated Everyone
Short levels suit quick breaks
cons: Has ads
Includes in-app purchases
Very similar to other sorting games, so it may feel repetitive
body: Each level gives you bolts stacked with colored nuts. You move nuts from one bolt to another, matching colors, until every bolt holds nuts of a single color.
It plays like other sorting puzzles but with a nuts-and-bolts theme. Levels begin easy and get trickier as more colors and fewer free spaces appear.
The game is free and supported by ads and optional purchases. It is a fit for players who like unwinding with a sorting puzzle and don't need much story or variety.
Nut-Sort-Color-Match-Game.author: editors

Altos-Odyssey.verdict: A smooth endless sandboarder where you chain flips and grinds across desert dunes.
Altos-Odyssey.bestFor: Players who want a relaxing endless runner with great visuals and simple one-touch controls.
pros: Easy one-finger controls: tap to jump, hold to flip
Beautiful desert scenery with changing weather and time of day
Free to play and rated Everyone
Goals give you something to work toward
cons: Has ads
Includes in-app purchases
Runs can feel similar over time
body: You ride a sandboard down endless dunes, jumping over rocks and chasms, grinding on ropes and chaining flips for points. A tap makes you jump, and holding it in the air makes you flip.
Each run is short, and a list of goals unlocks new characters and items. The mood is calmer than most runners, with a soft soundtrack and a gentle, scenic look.
It is free but shows ads and offers purchases. It suits anyone who likes short sessions and wants a runner that is relaxing rather than frantic.
Altos-Odyssey.author: editors

Subway-Surfers.verdict: A colorful endless runner where you dodge trains and collect coins while escaping an inspector.
Subway-Surfers.bestFor: Anyone who wants a quick, familiar runner that is free and easy to pick up.
pros: Simple swipe controls that are easy to learn
Free and rated Everyone 10+
Frequent updates with new locations and characters
Good for short sessions
cons: Ads appear regularly
Has in-app purchases for coins, keys and characters
Gameplay doesn't change much between runs
body: You run along train tracks, swiping to change lanes, jump and roll under obstacles. Along the way you collect coins, which you spend on characters and boards, and power-ups such as a jetpack.
Missions and events give each run some purpose, and a hoverboard can save you from one crash. The game is bright and fast, and the cartoon style keeps it light.
It is free with ads and optional purchases. It suits players of almost any age who want something quick to play, though anyone looking for depth may tire of it.
Subway-Surfers.author: editors

WorldBox.verdict: A sandbox where you create a world, place creatures and use god powers to see what happens.
WorldBox.bestFor: Players who enjoy experimenting and watching a world develop rather than following goals.
pros: Open-ended play with lots of powers to try
Pixel-art worlds that run on their own after you start them
Free to download and rated Everyone
Good for creative, experimental players
cons: Has ads
Some features require purchase
No set goals, which may feel aimless to some players
body: You begin with an empty map and shape land, add water and forests, and then place humans, elves, orcs and other creatures. They build villages, form kingdoms and sometimes go to war.
You can also use powers to cause rain, fire or disasters, and see what happens. There are no missions, so your enjoyment depends on how much you like experimenting and watching things play out.
The game is free with ads and in-app purchases, including a premium option. It suits players who like sandbox games and are happy making their own fun.
WorldBox.author: editors

TheoTown.verdict: A pixel-art city builder where you zone land, lay roads and keep your residents happy.
TheoTown.bestFor: City-building fans who want a free, detailed builder on their phone.
pros: Real city-building depth: zoning, services, power and budgets
Free to download and rated Everyone
Charming pixel-art style that runs on many devices
Lets you build at your own pace
cons: Has ads
Includes in-app purchases
Managing a large city can take some patience
body: You start with an empty plot and zone areas for homes, shops and industry, then add roads, power, water and services such as schools and fire stations. As your population grows, you need to balance your budget and keep citizens happy.
You can also deal with disasters and unlock new buildings as the town expands. There is no strict goal, so you can aim for a big metropolis or a neat small town.
It is free with ads and optional purchases. It is a good fit for players who like planning and managing a city over longer sessions.
TheoTown.author: editors

method: {site} picks Android games from Google Play and sorts them into lists by mood, player and play style, so you can find something worth downloading without scrolling the store for an hour.

The score out of 5 is our editors' judgment, not the Google Play star rating. It weighs how good and deep the game is, how fair its ads and in-app purchases are, how well it runs on an everyday phone and how long it stays fun. Editor's Choice marks the reviewed games we would suggest to almost anyone.

Star ratings, install counts, prices, age ratings and whether a game has ads or in-app purchases come straight from Google Play and are refreshed every day, so they can change from one visit to the next.
Every game is made by its own developer and downloads from Google Play. {site} is not affiliated with Google or with any game publisher.
Publishers do not pay for reviews or for a spot on a list.
We revisit the lists regularly. If a price, rating or detail looks out of date, tell us through the contact page.
